options.explanation: That is translocation.

options.text: The exchange of gases in leaves

questions.stem: Where does most transpiration take place?

options.explanation: Bark is waterproofed against loss.

options.text: Through stomata, mostly on the leaf's underside
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those absorb water; they do not lose it.
Petals are not the main site.

questions.stem: Which benefit keeps leaves from drooping?

options.explanation: Sugars are solutes, not the support mechanism here.
Wind would worsen drooping.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The cuticle limits loss; turgor stops the droop.

questions.stem: How does transpiration cool the leaf?

options.text: By shading the leaf from the sun
options.explanation: Nothing shades anything.

options.text: By conducting heat to the roots
options.explanation: Conduction downward is not the mechanism.
No cold gas exists; evaporation takes heat away.

options.text: Heat energy is lost from the leaves as water evaporates
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which mineral ions travel with the transpiration stream?

options.text: Ions such as nitrates dissolved in the rising water
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The stream carries dissolved ions.
Sugars ride the phloem.
Oxygen is not a soil mineral ion.

questions.stem: State three functions transpiration serves for the plant.
questions.modelAnswer: It draws water up to the leaves, cools them by evaporation, and transports mineral ions while keeping cells turgid.

questions.stem: Name the pore through which a single vapour loss event occurs.
questions.modelAnswer: One pore is a stoma; the plural is stomata.

questions.stem: Explain why wilting follows prolonged water shortage.
questions.modelAnswer: Because without enough water the cells lose turgor pressure, so the once-firm tissues can no longer hold the leaf upright.

questions.stem: A gardener mists a wilting plant's leaves at noon. Explain how misting helps briefly.
questions.modelAnswer: The mist raises humidity around the leaves, slowing further evaporation so the leaf loses water more slowly while the roots catch up.

questions.stem: How does increased wind speed affect transpiration?

options.explanation: Wind does not close pores directly.

options.text: It increases the rate by sweeping vapour away from the leaf
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Removal of vapour steepens the gradient, raising loss.
Air movement is one of the four factors.

questions.stem: Why does higher temperature raise the transpiration rate?

options.explanation: Warmer air can hold more vapour; the rate still rises.
No shrinking occurs.

options.text: Water molecules gain kinetic energy and diffuse out of the stomata more readily
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because stomata close in the heat
options.explanation: They open with light, not close with warmth here.

questions.stem: What happens to transpiration when humidity increases?

options.explanation: Extra outside vapour flattens the gradient.
No doubling rule exists.
Humidity is precisely one of the four dials.

options.text: The rate decreases, because the air outside the leaf holds more water molecules
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: How does light intensity raise the transpiration rate?

options.text: More stomata open, so vapour diffuses out of the leaf faster
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The named mechanism is stomatal opening.
Diffusion does the moving.
No thickening happens.

questions.stem: In still, dim, dry-cold conditions compared with a windy bright warm one, the rate is...

options.explanation: Some evaporation continues regardless.

options.text: Lower on every count, since each factor's decrease works oppositely
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Higher, because still air traps vapour near the leaf
options.explanation: Trapped vapour flattens the gradient, lowering loss.
All four dials have moved against the rate.

questions.stem: List the four factors affecting transpiration rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Air movement, humidity, temperature and light intensity.

questions.stem: State the humidity rule and its reason.
questions.modelAnswer: As humidity increases the rate decreases, because more water molecules outside the leaf weaken the diffusion gradient.

questions.stem: Explain why wind and humidity act on the same underlying cause.
questions.modelAnswer: Both change the concentration gradient between the leaf's interior and the surrounding air: wind steepens it by removing vapour, humidity flattens it by adding vapour.

questions.stem: A greenhouse grower wants faster transpiration for a water-hungry crop. Suggest two dial settings.
questions.modelAnswer: Increase air movement with fans and raise light intensity with lamps, both of which raise the rate.
